speaker: Soumith Chintala
title: The Gradient Podcast - Soumith Chintala: PyTorch
question: In machine learning research, why do established senior academics often dismiss promising new methods even after strong early results appear?
guest: I think there are a couple of things. One is a sunk cost fallacy, right? If you basically invested 10 years of your life into a certain expertise, you would want to give that a fair shot before you give up on it. The other thing is there are genuinely fads that come and go, and they last for longer than you would think. The older, more experienced people do see some of these fads come and go, and they want to make sure this new thing isn't really a fad. One example which I worked on is GANs. GANs came and went. If you talked to someone in 2017, they would look at you like a fool if you said GANs were a passing fad, because half the papers were being written about GANs. I stopped working on GANs at some point because I just thought they were so unstable, and it was not clear that they could be stabilized. So I shelved my work on GANs purely because I thought I'd wait a few years until someone figures this out. That's an example of a fad, so it's completely fair for people to have that skeptical position.

points.core: Senior researchers face sunk-cost bias after investing years mastering older methods.
points.note: Accept: sunk-cost fallacy, career investment in prior paradigms, reluctance to abandon decade-long expertise. Do not credit: generic claims that older people dislike change or vague institutional politics.

points.core: Experienced researchers have repeatedly watched major research fads last years before fading.
points.note: Accept: surviving prior hype cycles, seeing dominant trends like GANs eventually lose relevance over several years. Do not credit: vague references to hype without noting that fads persist for years.

points.core: Prolonged skepticism filters out fundamentally unstable techniques before committing research effort.
points.note: Accept: waiting for methods to stabilize or prove durable before switching, treating skepticism as a rational filter. Do not credit: claiming senior academics are simply wrong or overly conservative.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Several forces combine, and not all of them are irrational.

The rational part is that most "promising" early results in ML don't hold up. Benchmarks get overfit, baselines are under-tuned, and gains often vanish under replication, so a skeptical prior is usually correct. Senior researchers have seen many hyped methods fade, and that experience makes them discount early evidence.

The less rational part is investment and identity. Careers, grants, labs and reputations are built on a particular paradigm, so a new method threatens accumulated expertise. People also judge new work by the standards of their own framework: neural networks were long dismissed for lacking theoretical guarantees that kernel methods and graphical models offered, even as empirical results improved. Deep learning before 2012 is the classic case, with papers rejected partly because reviewers considered the approach already discredited.

There is also a structural factor: early results typically appear on narrow tasks, and it is unclear whether they will scale, which leaves room for motivated reasoning in either direction.

The premise is also only partly true: many senior academics adopt new methods quickly, as the rapid uptake of transformers showed.

points.why: The response links resistance to the expertise and career capital senior researchers have accumulated in an established paradigm.
quotes: Careers, grants, labs and reputations are built on a particular paradigm, so a new method threatens accumulated expertise.

points.why: The response says senior researchers have seen many hyped methods fade but omits that major fads can persist for years before fading.
The response gives rational grounds for discounting early evidence but does not connect sustained skepticism to deferring research investment until a method proves stable or durable.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Established machine learning researchers often dismiss promising new methods due to a mix of hard-won empirical skepticism, theoretical commitments, and institutional sunk costs. Having watched decades of hyped breakthroughs fail to generalize beyond narrow benchmarks, senior academics know how easily strong early results can stem from hyperparameter tuning, subtle data leakage, or extra compute rather than genuine algorithmic progress. Many also prize mathematical guarantees, interpretability, and domain structure, making poorly understood, scale-driven approaches—as captured in Richard Sutton’s “bitter lesson”—feel like unprincipled engineering tricks rather than real science. 

At the same time, Thomas Kuhn’s paradigm inertia applies strongly: senior scholars have built labs, courses, grant pipelines, and reputations around established frameworks such as kernel methods, probabilistic graphical models, or symbolic reasoning. Embracing a disruptive paradigm depreciates decades of specialized expertise and shifts advantage toward newcomers or compute-rich industry labs. Because most flashy ML claims genuinely do fizzle out upon closer scrutiny, rational methodological caution easily blurs into cognitive conservatism, causing veterans to mistake true foundational shifts for passing fads.

points.why: The response ties reluctance to switch paradigms to the prospect of devaluing decades of specialized expertise.
quotes: Embracing a disruptive paradigm depreciates decades of specialized expertise

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise holds only partly. Senior researchers do sometimes resist new methods. The classic case is neural networks, which were widely dismissed until AlexNet in 2012. But many senior figures also adopted deep learning and transformers quickly, and much of their skepticism turns out to be justified.

When resistance happens, a few things usually drive it. Early results are often fragile. They can rely on narrow benchmarks, heavy tuning, weak baselines or more compute, and many "breakthroughs" don't replicate. Experienced researchers have watched hype cycles collapse before, so they discount early wins. Their judgment also rests on years of investment in particular frameworks, such as kernel methods, Bayesian approaches or theory-first work. A method that works without clear theory can look like unprincipled engineering to them, and admitting it works can make their own expertise less valuable. Institutions add to this, because reviewers, grant panels and hiring committees reward work within the existing standards. Finally, the "Planck's principle" effect is real but modest: studies of science suggest fields do sometimes move forward as newcomers enter, rather than through established figures changing their minds.

So the resistance is a mix of reasonable caution and status-quo bias, and it usually gives way once results hold up at scale.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Established senior academics often dismiss promising new machine learning methods due to a mix of earned skepticism, methodological standards, and institutional inertia. Having watched decades of hyped approaches fail to reproduce, overfit narrow benchmarks, or collapse outside toy settings, veteran researchers naturally treat striking early results as likely artifacts until proven robust across diverse tasks and scales. Moreover, breakthroughs in machine learning frequently arrive as messy empirical hacks lacking clean theory or thorough ablations, which clashes with senior scholars' preference for principled, mathematically grounded explanations. At the same time, career incentives and cognitive lock-in play a major role: established leaders have invested years building labs, reputations, and grant pipelines around prevailing paradigms, creating subtle blind spots toward approaches that render their specialized expertise less central. Combined with the sheer volume of modern ML papers—which forces senior figures to rely on quick heuristics when filtering new work—genuine paradigm shifts are often underestimated until overwhelming practical utility makes them impossible to ignore.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Strong early results can show that a method works in a particular setup while leaving open whether the gains survive stronger baselines, equal compute budgets, or independent replication. Senior researchers have often seen promising results fade under those checks, so some skepticism is warranted.

But experience can also make it harder to recognize a genuine change. Researchers build their intuitions around problems and methods that have worked for years. A new approach may succeed where those intuitions predict failure, or solve a problem that established benchmarks undervalue. Familiar methods also have an institutional advantage. Reviewers know how to assess them, and labs have expertise and infrastructure built around them.

The distinction is whether the skeptic can say what evidence would change their mind. Asking for a specific test can help establish the result. Moving the goalposts after each successful test can keep a promising idea from getting a fair hearing.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Strong early results can show that a method works in one setting while leaving open why it works and how widely it will apply. Researchers who have seen apparent breakthroughs fade when someone tunes the baseline more carefully or tests on a different dataset have good reason to ask for replication.

Seniority can also make skepticism harder to revise. Years spent developing a successful approach shape which problems seem important and which explanations seem plausible. A competing method may challenge those judgments while making hard-won expertise less valuable. That can lead someone to demand stronger evidence for a new approach than they would for a familiar one, even in good faith.

One way to distinguish caution from dismissal is to ask what evidence would change the critic’s mind. A specific concern that narrows as evidence accumulates suggests caution. A standard that keeps shifting suggests the skepticism may have other roots.
